picked.t: Da Nang accommodation options cater to different travel needs
picked.body: For some visitors, a Da Nang trip starts with an early walk along My Khe Beach. Others prioritize food, sightseeing or time with family. The best accommodation therefore depends less on the number of facilities or the lowest advertised rate than on three factors: group size, length of stay and how much time guests expect to spend at the property. Location and hotels for shorter stays Travelers should first choose an area based on their itinerary before comparing accommodation. Those planning to swim or walk along the shore may prefer My Khe Beach, while visitors focused on the Museum of Cham Sculpture, city dining and walks along Bach Dang Street may find the central area more convenient. For mixed itineraries, comparing travel times to frequently visited places can help identify the most practical location. Everyday convenience, such as easy access to breakfast or a quick trip back with tired children, may matter more than proximity to a single attraction. For couples, solo travelers and small families on short visits, a beachfront hotel can make the coast part of the daily routine while providing services such as breakfast, housekeeping and reception support. A comfortable room may be sufficient for guests who spend most of their time exploring the city. Before booking, travelers should check the property's exact location and beach access, bed arrangements and included services. Apartments when daily routines matter For longer stays, a kitchen, laundry facilities and a separate workspace can be more useful than hotel services. Self-catering apartments can suit families with young children, remote workers and travelers who prefer to prepare some meals themselves. Layouts vary from studios with kitchenettes to larger units with separate bedrooms, living areas and full kitchens. Travelers should check the appliances and cooking equipment provided, laundry arrangements and cleaning schedules. For extended stays, they should also confirm whether electricity, water and other charges are included. Remote workers should verify the availability of a suitable workspace and reliable internet connection rather than relying solely on a general Wi-Fi listing. Whole-house villas for larger groups For larger families or groups of friends, an entire villa can provide shared living space while allowing guests to stay under one roof. Hanami Villa Da Nang at 276/7 Ngu Hanh Son Street is one example. According to its operator, the property is rented as a whole and has six bedrooms, shared living areas, a private pool, two kitchens, a cinema room, a steam room and a rooftop area. The operator says it can accommodate up to 16 guests. The villa is in a residential area rather than directly on the beachfront. It is managed by Nami Stay , which provides local support during guests' stays. For larger rentals, travelers should check the floor plan, bed allocation, stairs and bathroom access, particularly when traveling with people with limited mobility. Families should also ask about pool safety and other measures before arrival. Price comparisons should cover the full stay rather than the advertised nightly rate alone. Travelers should compare the same dates and group size while checking taxes, mandatory fees, deposits, cleaning or utility charges, cancellation terms and extra-person fees. For villas, they should also confirm whether the booking provides exclusive use of the property. Weather is another consideration. When rain disrupts outdoor plans, indoor communal space can become particularly useful for families and groups. Ultimately, a beachfront hotel can suit shorter stays centered on sightseeing and the coast, an apartment can support longer-term daily routines, while a whole-house villa can give larger groups more shared space. The best choice is the one whose location, layout, services and booking terms match the travelers and their plans, rather than simply the property that looks most appealing in photographs.

picked.t: Why are Korean visitors to Vietnam declining?
picked.body: Vietnam welcomed 17.7 million international visitors in the first nine months, up almost 15% year-on-year, the General Statistics Office reported. South Korea ranked second, after mainland China, with 3 million arrivals, but was the only top-10 market to record a decline, down about 5%. Korean arrivals also fell 5% in 2025, when total arrivals hit a record of more than 21 million. South Koreans made over 19 million overseas trips in the first eight months, up 2%, according to the Korea Tourism Organization. Martin Koerner, commercial director of Anam Group, which manages two resorts in Mui Ne and Cam Ranh, says Korean demand is still growing but shifting elsewhere. Yanolja Research found that only three of the 12 most-visited destinations for Koreans grew in the first half. Japan rose 18.6% to 5.6 million visits, 40% of Korean outbound travelers. Mainland China rose 16%, while Macau grew 0.7%. The other nine destinations, mostly in Southeast Asia and the U.S., all declined. Vietnam fell more than 2%, and Thailand dropped the most, at 24%. Pham Hai Quynh, director of the Asia Tourism Development Institute, attributes the decline partly to growing competition from China and Japan. Quynh says Japan offers a good exchange rate, easy transport and quality service. China has attractive tour prices, visa-free entry for Koreans since late 2025 and more direct flights. A weak won is a factor. The currency fell to 1,536 won per U.S. dollar on June 3, its lowest since 2009, and now sits around 1,350. Korea JoongAng Daily reports that the weak currency is changing how South Koreans travel. They are shopping less, opting for Airbnb-style rentals over luxury hotels. Hanatour, one of South Korea's largest travel companies, says Korean travelers used to favor cheap tours with shopping stops. Now they choose pricier packages without shopping to cut down on extra spending. However, travel spending in Japan continues to rise, as the weak yen makes the destination more affordable. In 2025, South Korean visitors spent a record $5.7 billion in Japan. Koerner adds that beyond cost, the convenience of the trip also shapes Korean choices. A flight of two to three hours to Japan or China beats a six-hour trip to Southeast Asia. "In this context, Vietnam's edge as a low-cost destination no longer creates a big enough gap to hold on to Korean visitors," Quynh says. Saturation is another problem. Quynh says a destination's life cycle lasts three to four years, after which travelers seek something new. Da Nang, Nha Trang and Phu Quoc have been promoted in Korea since around 2023, and golf and spa packages have grown familiar. Fewer flights have hurt too. Higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict led Korean airlines, mainly low-cost carriers, to cut 1,000 flights between April and June. Yanolja Research also says Vietnam's image has been linked to Cambodian scam compounds. Negative sentiment toward Vietnam once reached 18%. To win Koreans back, Quynh says Vietnam should refresh its image, rely less on cheap beach holidays, and develop cultural, ecological and wellness products. He also urges more promotion in Busan, Daegu and Gwangju cities. According to ET News , Vietnam remains the most popular Southeast Asian destination among South Koreans. Koerner says Vietnam needs to offer new experiences to bring back Korean travelers, many of whom have already visited the country. He states destinations, airlines, hotels, travel companies and online travel agencies should work together on packages with competitive prices and appealing experiences. Promotions also need to come sooner, as Korean travelers book just weeks before departure rather than months ahead. "The most important question is how Vietnam can beat its rivals and become the top choice at the moment travelers decide to book," he says.

picked.t: HCMC teen with IELTS 9.0 and top English awards for gifted students chooses teaching career
picked.body: Nguyen Tuan Phong is a former English major at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted in Ho Chi Minh City. He is currently enrolled in the university's English language teacher education program. He said he began considering a career in teaching early in 10th grade, after being selected for the national English competition team and winning second prize. The achievement motivated him but also brought considerable pressure. Phong repeatedly questioned whether he could continue improving and maintain his performance. Encouraged and inspired by the teachers who coached the competition team, he gradually regained his confidence and went on to win first prize in the competition for two consecutive years. "I also want to become a friendly teacher with strong professional knowledge who inspires students, just like the teachers I have learned from," Phong said. Phong took the IELTS test in 11th grade to strengthen his university application. Because the test came immediately after the national English competition, he did not have much time to prepare and aimed for a score of 8.0. He was therefore surprised to receive a perfect score. "I couldn't believe my eyes. I thought the sheet showing a score of 9.0 was just a sample result. Only after reading it carefully did I confirm that it was actually mine," he said. Phong said he had been exposed to English since the age of four and continued taking classes at language centers until the end of middle school. Initially, he was eager to learn English so he could watch foreign reality shows, movies, and cartoons. Over time, he shifted toward scientific content and materials related to his school curriculum. English, to him, became a "gateway" that opened up a more diverse and expansive world. Phong believes that practical application is essential to mastering a language. He regularly practices speaking English with classmates and native speakers whenever he has the opportunity. In his view, learning a foreign language requires perseverance, and every small improvement deserves recognition. "Don't put too much pressure on yourself or set too many goals. Haste makes waste, and the more stressed you are, the harder it becomes to absorb new knowledge," Phong said. Tran Kim Duyen, head of the foreign languages department at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted, coached Phong for several years. She described him as a well-rounded student who demonstrated creative thinking, independent learning skills, and a willingness to learn from teachers and peers without becoming arrogant. "Phong is confident, independent and always willing to support those around him. He also helps teachers organize extracurricular activities," she said. Building on his high school experience, Phong hopes to take part in a wide range of activities during his four years at university while striving for strong academic results. He aims to become an English teacher at the high school level. Vietnamese students currently take the same national high school graduation exams, but universities maintain their own admission standards. Institutions are allowed to award additional points, or grant direct admission, to applicants for academic awards, language certificates such as IELTS or SAT, or extracurricular achievements. However, the Ministry of Education and Training recently proposed eliminating university admission bonus points for IELTS certificates and excellent student awards starting next year.
